acts.title: One idea, stepped back twice
steps: If he crashes the plane, he will kill somebody.
If he crashed the plane, he would kill somebody.
SECOND — step back once. Past form in the if clause, would in the result.
If he had crashed the plane, he would have killed somebody.
THIRD — step back again. Past perfect in the if clause, would have in the result.
If he hadn’t taught himself to fly, nobody would have heard of him.
The negative works the same way in both halves.
Had he crashed the plane, he would have killed somebody.
Formal option: drop if and put had first.

acts.title: The last outlaw
text: Colton Harris-Moore was nineteen when the police finally caught him, in a stolen boat, in the Bahamas. By then he was suspected of more than a hundred thefts across two countries, and he had a Facebook page with tens of thousands of followers. He was known as the barefoot bandit, because he often carried out his robberies with no shoes on.

The part that made him famous was not the theft. It was the flying. He had never had a lesson. He taught himself from information he found on the internet, took a small plane and flew it, badly, until it ran out of fuel. He did this five times. He crash-landed every time, and every time he walked away.

If he had come down in a town rather than a field, he would almost certainly have killed somebody, and the story would have ended very differently. If any of his victims had been hurt, nobody would have set up a fan page. As it was, none of them were, and thousands of people online treated him as a kind of hero.

The interesting question is what would have happened to a different Colton. He grew up with almost nothing, left school early and was in trouble by thirteen. If somebody had reached him at that age, he might never have taken the first boat. If he had had the money for lessons, he would probably have become a pilot; the skill was clearly there.

He was sentenced to just over six years, and the court ordered that any money he made from the story should go to his victims. If you asked him now whether it was worth it, he would probably say no. But nobody asked him anything much at thirteen.

items.s: Colton had taken flying lessons before he flew a plane.
He crash-landed every plane he took.
One of his victims was seriously injured.
He had a large following online.
The writer suggests he might have become a pilot in different circumstances.
The court let him keep the money made from his story.

tts: Let’s move on to a new film which has just been announced, about the life and crimes of the barefoot bandit.
Apparently the money he makes from the film will be going straight to his victims, but can it be right to make films which celebrate somebody’s crimes?
I think it’s a fascinating story. The biggest thing with him is that the story was just so entertaining. Everyone wanted to know what would happen next.
And lots of people loved the idea of him teaching himself to fly.
But he wasn’t really somebody to be admired, was he? If he had crashed the plane in a town, he would probably have killed someone.

There are examples of criminals who actually did some good, though. Take Ned Kelly. He was arrested for murder, but he claimed he hadn’t done it and escaped. He and three others robbed banks, but they were kind to the people who worked in them.

use: If he hadn’t…, he wouldn’t have…

items.sit: You are saying that one past action caused everything else.
o: If he hadn’t taught himself to fly, nobody would have heard of him.
If he didn’t teach himself to fly, nobody would hear of him.
If he wouldn’t have taught himself to fly, nobody would have heard of him.

items.sit: You are saying what you personally would not have done.
o: I would never have got on that plane.
I would never got on that plane.
I never would have get on that plane.

items.sit: You are asking somebody to imagine a different past.
o: What if they had caught him at thirteen?
What if they caught him at thirteen, would it change?
What if they would have caught him at thirteen?

items.sit: You want to say it formally, without using “if”.
o: Had I known, I would have said something.
Had if I known, I would have said something.
If had I known, I would have said something.

items.sit: You are talking about now, not about the past.
o: If I knew him, I’d say something.
If I had known him, I’d say something.
If I would know him, I’d say something.

items.sit: You want a softer result than “would have”.
o: He might have become a pilot.

write.q: Write about a turning point — in your own life, in your family, or in a story you know. Use the third conditional at least four times, including one negative and one with might have. Then add one second conditional about how things are now.
plan: what would have happened if it hadn’t
the softer version with might have
write.model: If I hadn’t missed a train in 2016, I would probably still be working in the same shop. I was going to an interview in Astana and I got to the platform four minutes late. If the next train had been full, I would have gone home and given up. It wasn’t, and I arrived ninety minutes late and apologized for six of them. They offered me the job the same afternoon, which I still do not entirely understand. If the manager had been anybody else, I might never have got in the door. Had I known how much that morning would change, I would probably have been too nervous to leave the flat. As it is, if I met that manager now, I am not sure I would know what to say to him.

speak.q: Talk for about a minute about one thing that could easily have gone differently in your life. Say what would have happened, and use might have at least once to keep it honest.
speak.model: If I hadn’t missed a train in 2016, I’d probably still be in the same shop. I got to the platform four minutes late. If the next one had been full, I would have gone home and given up. It wasn’t, so I arrived ninety minutes late and got the job anyway. If the manager had been anybody else, I might never have got through the door.
